questions.q: A coach says 'Watch the next bird.' What will you see?

options.text: A live pigeon released from a box
A clay target thrown by a trap
A bird-shaped paper target on a board

questions.explain: 'Bird' is shooters' slang for a clay target; the FITASC rules forbid shooting at live animals.

questions.q: What does a shotgun fire?
questions.explain: The shot leaves the muzzle as a small cloud of pellets, so the shooter points ahead of the moving target.

questions.q: Which statement about Compak® Sporting is correct?

options.text: A compact version on one field, stations in a line
It is a course of stands spread through a forest
It is shot only at live game birds in the field
It uses a single trap and a single station

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting brings Sporting™-style targets onto one small field with five stations and six traps.

questions.q: What do you shoot at in clay shooting?

options.text: Live birds released from a box
Clay targets thrown by a trap
Paper targets fixed on a board

questions.explain: You shoot only at artificial targets thrown by a trap. Shooting at live animals is forbidden.

questions.q: What is a trap?

options.text: A shotgun with a short barrel
The referee who runs the stand

questions.explain: A trap is the machine that throws a target into the air or rolls it along the ground.

questions.q: Why does a shooter point the gun ahead of a moving target?

options.text: The shot needs time to reach the target
The referee asks all shooters to do it
It keeps the gun from touching the target

questions.explain: The target moves and the shot takes time to get there, so the gun points where the target will be a moment later.

questions.q: Where may you load the gun?

options.text: Anywhere at the ground, if the gun points at the ground
Only on the stand, pointing down the range, once shooting is allowed
On the way to the stand, so you are ready when called

questions.explain: Cartridges go in only on the stand, with the gun pointing down the range, after the referee or instructor allows shooting.

questions.q: What must you do before turning round on the stand?

options.text: Open the gun and take out all cartridges, fired or not
Put the safety catch on and keep the gun closed
Take out only the unfired cartridges, then close the gun

questions.explain: You turn round only with the gun open and empty; a safety catch is no substitute for an open gun.

questions.q: The gun clicks but does not fire. What should the shooter do?

options.text: Open it at once to see what went wrong
Turn round and show the gun to the coach
Stay put, gun down the range, and wait for the referee
Put the safety on and call for the target again

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require the shooter to stay put until the referee inspects; opening or touching the safety first scores zero.

questions.q: How many cartridges may a semi-automatic hold?

options.text: As many as the magazine takes

questions.explain: In both disciplines a semi-automatic may hold no more than two cartridges.

questions.q: How is a semi-automatic carried between stands?

options.text: Closed, with the safety catch on
With the action open, muzzle up or down
On a sling over the shoulder, unloaded
With one cartridge in, safety on

questions.explain: Guns are carried open, semi-automatics with the action open, muzzles straight up or down; slings are not allowed.

questions.q: Someone shouts “Cease fire!”. What is the interpreter’s first job?

options.text: Repeat “Stop!” loudly and check that the guns are open
Explain to the guests why shooting has stopped
Ask the coach quietly what has happened
Wait until a guest asks what is going on

questions.explain: An emergency stop is repeated at once; explanations come only when all guns are open.

questions.q: Lightning is close and the referee has paused shooting. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the gun closed and wait on the stand
Open and unload the gun, then shelter in a building
Shelter under the nearest tall tree with your gun

questions.explain: During any pause the gun is open and empty, and in lightning you leave the open ground for a building.

questions.q: Who must wear hearing protection at a competition?

options.text: Only the shooter who is on the stand
Shooters and referees, but not spectators
Everyone near the layout, spectators too

questions.explain: The rules of both disciplines name shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the layout.

questions.q: Your shooter walks onto the stand without safety glasses. How do the rules treat him?

options.text: He gets a warning and may shoot
He may shoot if the coach agrees

questions.explain: In both disciplines a shooter without eye or ear protection on the stand is treated as absent and may not shoot.

questions.q: Which gives the most hearing protection when many shots are fired?

options.text: Earplugs and ear muffs worn together
Electronic muffs with the volume turned up
Earplugs pushed in loosely, for comfort

questions.explain: Plugs and muffs together protect most, as long as both fit well.

questions.q: What is the advantage of electronic ear muffs?

options.text: They soften the shot but let voices through
They block all sound, voices included

questions.explain: You are protected from the bang and still hear the referee’s commands.

questions.q: Which shorts are allowed at a FITASC competition?

options.text: Any sports shorts, as long as the shirt has sleeves
Bermuda-style shorts, ending no more than 5 cm above the knee
Short shorts in Compak® Sporting, but not in Sporting™
No shorts of any length, in either discipline

questions.explain: Short shorts are banned in both disciplines; long Bermuda-style shorts are accepted.

questions.q: Why are electronic ear muffs a good choice for an interpreter?

options.text: They soften the shot but let voices through
They are not required for interpreters

questions.explain: Hearing protection is compulsory near a layout, and electronic muffs let you hear the coach and referee.

questions.q: When may you step onto the stand?

options.text: As soon as the previous shooter has fired his last shot
When the stand is free and it is your turn
Together with the shooter before you, to save time

questions.explain: You step up only once the previous shooter has left the stand and it is your turn.

questions.q: May a friend give a shooter advice during a competition?

options.text: Yes, if he whispers it between targets
Only if the friend is a qualified coach
No: it counts as coaching and is penalised

questions.explain: Coaching during a competition is forbidden for everyone, coaches included: the shooter gets a yellow card.

questions.q: A loud phone call behind the stand clearly disturbs the shooter at the moment of the shot. What may the referee decide?

options.text: No Bird: the target is thrown again
Nothing, phones are not in the rules

questions.explain: If the referee sees the shooter was clearly disturbed, the target is a No Bird.

questions.q: How long do you have to call for a target in Compak® Sporting?
questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting a shooter has at most 10 seconds; the first breach is a warning, a repeat in the same round is penalised.

questions.q: Where does the interpreter stand while the guest is shooting?

options.text: Beside the shooter, to see his face
In front of the stand, to see the target
Behind the stand, out of any line of the barrels

questions.explain: Everyone who is not shooting waits behind the stand, cage or F.A.L.; beside or in front of the stand you are in or near the swing of the barrels.

questions.q: When is the right moment to pass on the coach’s comment?

options.text: While the shooter is calling for the target
Between the call and the shot, in a whisper
As soon as the coach has finished speaking
Once the gun is open after a target or pair

questions.explain: The shooter’s routine must not be interrupted; speak only once the gun is open.

questions.q: Who decides whether a target was hit?

options.text: The squad, by a show of hands
The referee, and the referee alone
The shooter, by checking the pieces

questions.explain: Only the referee decides; the squad does not step in unless the referee asks.

questions.q: How do you properly disagree with a referee’s decision?

options.text: At once on the stand: raise your hand and say “protest”
After the round, with a post on social media
By arguing until the referee changes his mind

questions.explain: A protest is made at once, on the stand; arguing afterwards counts as an attempt to influence.

questions.q: A squad-mate loudly tells the referee he is wrong about a hit. How do the rules see this?

options.text: As useful information for the referee
As a formal protest by the squad
As an attempt to influence the referee
As normal chat with no consequence

questions.explain: Others openly criticising a ruling without the referee’s permission count as an attempt to influence; only the shooter concerned may protest.

questions.q: What can happen after aggressive behaviour towards the referee?

options.text: Nothing, if the shooter apologises later
The jury may expel the shooter
The shooter shoots the next target again

questions.explain: The referee reports it to the jury, which may expel the shooter from the competition.

questions.q: During a competition round the coach asks you to tell the shooter “more lead on the crosser”. What do you do?

options.text: Whisper it quickly while he loads
Pass it on after the next target
Decline politely: that would be coaching
Ask the referee to pass it on

questions.explain: Coaching during competition is forbidden and the shooter would get a yellow card. The rules do not say whether relaying advice is allowed, so stay on the safe side.

questions.q: What do the FITASC rulebooks say about interpreters?

options.text: They may stand on the stand
Nothing: it is an open question

questions.explain: The rulebooks do not mention interpreters, so their exact position in competition is an open question for FITASC.

questions.q: In training, the coach says “Not bad, but you stopped the gun.” How do you translate?

options.text: Fully and in the same tone, both parts
Only the praise, to keep the guest happy
Only the fault, to save time
Add your own tip on how to fix it

questions.explain: You neither soften nor inflate: the whole message, in the coach’s tone, with nothing of your own.

questions.q: Where should you stand during a training session on a Sporting™ stand?

options.text: Beside the shooter, to see his eyes
Behind the shooter, next to the coach
In front of the cage, facing him
Next to the trap, to watch the target

questions.explain: From behind, out of the barrels’ line, you see what the coach sees and stay safe; beside or in front is dangerous.

questions.q: What is chuchotage?

options.text: A written translation of the rules
Whispering the translation into the ear

questions.explain: Chuchotage means whispering the translation into the shooter’s ear while the coach keeps talking. Consecutive interpreting is the pause-and-speak mode: the coach says a sentence, pauses, and you translate it.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, how long does a shooter have to call after the previous station’s target was shot?
questions.explain: Compak® Sporting gives at most 10 seconds to call; Sporting™ allows at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles.

questions.q: In Sporting™ the target leaves five seconds after the referee’s signal. What is the referee’s decision?

options.text: Zero, because the shooter called too early
A warning for the trapper only

questions.explain: A target must leave within three seconds of the referee’s signal; a target released later is a No Bird and is thrown again.

questions.q: In competition, when may a shooter load the gun?

options.text: While walking to the next stand
On the stand, after the referee allows it
As soon as the coach says so

questions.explain: Loading is allowed only on the stand, gun pointing down the range, and only once the referee has said shooting may start.

questions.q: Which words start a formal protest on the stand?
questions.explain: Both rulebooks name “protest” or “appeal” with a raised hand, at once; “No Bird” is the referee’s word.

questions.q: The coach shouts “Smoked it!” after a shot. What happened?

options.text: Only smoke came off: a zero
The target was destroyed: a perfect hit
The target was a flash target

questions.explain: In coach slang “smoked it” is a perfect hit; in the rules “only dust or smoke” is a zero. The meanings are opposite.

questions.q: The referee says “Lost.” What does it mean?

options.text: The target flew out of sight
The shooter ran out of time
The target left its usual line
A miss: the target is a zero

questions.explain: “Lost” is the scoring word for a miss (zero), not something lost.

questions.q: A French guest says he loves shooting “en battue”. What does he mean?

options.text: Driven game (birds driven over the guns)
The thin battue target that turns
A target thrown as part of a pair
A target that breaks into dust

questions.explain: French “en battue” (Italian “in battuta”) means driven game; the battue target is a separate thing.

questions.q: A British coach says “It’s a true pair.” What is the FITASC term?
questions.explain: “True pair” is the British and American name for two targets released together, a FITASC simultaneous double.

questions.q: A coach says 'Raise the comb'. Which part does he mean?

options.text: The top of the stock, where the cheek rests
The small bead at the end of the rib
The choke tube at the muzzle

questions.explain: The comb is the top of the stock; raising it lifts the eye above the rib.

questions.q: What must a gun with a release trigger carry?

options.text: A red-painted barrel to warn others
A large 'R' sticker on the stock

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require the 'R' warning sticker, on a fluorescent background, on the outer side of the buttstock.

questions.q: What is the barrel selector for?

options.text: To take the barrels off the action
To change the choke in the barrel
To throw the fired cases out
To choose which barrel fires first

questions.explain: The selector, often combined with the safety, sets the order of the barrels.

questions.q: What do the ejectors do when you open the gun?

options.text: They throw out the fired cases
They lock the barrels to the action
They set which barrel fires first
They soften the recoil of the shot

questions.explain: Ejectors throw out fired cases; simpler extractors only lift them a little.

questions.q: Which part do you take off first to remove the barrels?
questions.explain: The fore-end holds the barrels on the action; once it is off, the barrels come off.

questions.q: What does a coach mean by 'Break your gun'?

options.text: Take the gun apart into pieces
Open the gun on its hinge
Clean the barrels of the gun

questions.explain: On a shooting ground 'break' means opening the gun on its hinge so it cannot fire.

questions.q: Who approves the layouts for an international Sporting™ competition?
questions.explain: National layouts are approved by the national federation, international ones by FITASC.

questions.q: What certificate must the chief referee hold?

options.text: A club membership card, nothing more
A national coaching licence from his club
None: any experienced shooter can do it

questions.explain: Stand referees need a national certificate; the chief referee needs an international one from FITASC.

questions.q: During an argument about a referee's decision, someone shows ClayArena's rules summary. How much does it count?

options.text: It counts more than the official FITASC text
It is only a guide; the FITASC text decides
It is binding, but only in Compak® Sporting
It replaces the referee's decision on the stand

questions.explain: A summary helps you understand the rules, but the referee and jury apply the official FITASC text.

questions.q: A national competition is announced. Which rules will apply?

options.text: FITASC rules only, word for word
The rules named in its programme

questions.explain: National competitions follow FITASC rules or the country's own rules; the programme says which.

questions.q: A federation hands a competition to a club. Who stays responsible for applying the rules?

options.text: The club, and only the club
The federation that handed it over
The shooters who enter the event

questions.explain: A federation may delegate an event to a club, but it stays fully responsible to FITASC.

questions.q: What does the jury do at an international competition?

options.text: Throws the targets from the traps

questions.explain: The jury checks that the rules are applied, settles technical problems, hears appeals and sets penalties.

questions.q: How many targets does one Sporting™ layout give, and how are they split?
questions.explain: Each layout type gives 15 singles plus 5 doubles, which is 25 targets.

questions.q: In what order does a squad shoot at a stand?

options.text: Doubles first, then singles, in a fixed order
Singles first, then doubles, in rotation
Each shooter shoots the whole stand in one go
The shooters agree on the order themselves

questions.explain: Singles come first, then doubles, in rotation, unless the jury decides otherwise.

questions.q: Leaving the stand, a shooter sees that a hit was marked as a miss. What should he do?

options.text: Wait for the end of the round and appeal to the jury
Tell the referee at once; the referee decides

questions.explain: Scores are checked when leaving each stand; the referee alone decides, and there is no appeal afterwards.

questions.q: How many targets does an international Sporting™ competition have?
questions.explain: An international event is 200 targets, shot in eight rounds of 25.

questions.q: A coach says “Go to stand two.” What does “stand” mean here?
questions.explain: In Sporting™ a stand is the 1 m place where the shooter stands. It is not the whole ground.

questions.q: How are the traps of a Sporting™ stand identified?

options.text: By numbers 1 to 6, counted from the right
By colours painted on each machine
By letters A, B, C, D from left to right
By the name of the person releasing them

questions.explain: The letters A, B, C, D are read from left to right as seen from the stand, and the menu and scorecard use them.

questions.q: In Sporting™, how does the shooting order work in a squad?

options.text: It rotates at each stand and for the doubles
It is fixed for the whole day

questions.explain: Squads of six are drawn, and the order rotates at each stand and also for the doubles.

questions.q: How many traps and stations does one Compak® Sporting field have?
questions.explain: Traps A to F and stations 1 to 5.

questions.q: The shooter on station 5 has finished his menu. Where does he go?

options.text: To the referee to sign the sheet

questions.explain: He becomes the waiting shooter behind station 1 while everyone else moves one station to the right.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, how may the gun be held when you call for the target?

options.text: Free: it may already be mounted
Only low, below the line on the vest
Only on the shoulder, muzzles up

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free, but you always shoot with the gun mounted. The low gun with a vest line is a Sporting™ rule.

questions.q: In a squad of six, where is the sixth shooter while the others shoot?

options.text: Next to the referee at station 5

questions.explain: The waiting shooter stands behind station 1 and steps onto it after each rotation.

questions.q: What is the Firing Angle Limiter for?

options.text: It limits the swing and stops stepping forward
It measures the speed of each target thrown
It holds the cartridges for the whole round
It releases the targets on the shooter's call

questions.explain: It is a safety frame at each station limiting sideways and vertical swing.

questions.q: On a Compak, the first target of each double is…

options.text: any target the shooter wants to start with
always the target from trap A
a target shown only on the shooter's request
the last target shot at the previous station

questions.explain: The menu chains the stations: each double begins with the target that ended the station before.

questions.q: In still air, what must each Compak® Sporting target do?
questions.explain: In still air each target must pass over the rectangle at some point of its flight.

questions.q: Where is the line of stations on a Compak?

options.text: 4 to 8 m behind side AD, parallel to it
Inside the rectangle, near side BC
On the tower, behind trap F

questions.explain: The stations stand in a line 4 to 8 m behind side AD, with station 3 opposite its middle.

questions.q: In Sporting™, how long may it take for the target to leave after the referee's signal?
questions.explain: A target released later than three seconds is a No Bird.

questions.q: What is the fixed delay of a sonopull in Compak® Sporting?

options.text: It is set by each shooter

questions.explain: The sonopull must apply a fixed, unchangeable delay of 0.5 seconds.

questions.q: You are on a stand with voice release and the shooter is ready. What do you do?

options.text: Give the shooter a last tip aloud
Ask the trapper to wait a moment
Repeat the call word for him
Stay silent; whisper only between targets

questions.explain: Your voice can trigger the microphone and release a target nobody called.

questions.q: Which special targets must a Sporting™ menu show?

options.text: Only the colours of the targets
90 mm, 70 mm, 60 mm, battue or rabbit

questions.explain: The menu must list the traps in order and any special target types.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, with which target does each double start?

options.text: Always the target from trap A
A new target that was not shown before
The last target shot at the previous station
Any target the shooter chooses first

questions.explain: The doubles chain across stations: each begins with the last target of the station before.

questions.q: Which type of double exists only in Sporting™?
questions.explain: Compak® Sporting doubles are on report or simultaneous; rafale is a Sporting™ double.

questions.q: What happens if you come to the stand without hearing protection or safety glasses?

options.text: You may shoot, but you get a warning
You are treated as absent and may not shoot
The referee gives you a spare set

questions.explain: In both disciplines a shooter without hearing protection or safety glasses is treated as absent, and the lateness rules apply.

questions.q: Where may you check that your gun works?

options.text: On the first competition stand, before the round
Anywhere on the ground, if the area is clear
At a special test stand, if the ground has one

questions.explain: Test shots on a competition stand are not allowed in either discipline; use the test stand.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting shot by squad, a shooter arrives after the first shooter has called for the first target. What happens?

options.text: He gets 25 zeros for that round
He shoots the round alone later without penalty

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting shot by squad, arriving after the first call costs 25 zeros for the round. For a reason outside your control, you can appeal to the jury in writing on the same day.

questions.q: What is the largest number of shooters in a squad?
questions.explain: In both Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting a squad has at most 6 shooters.

questions.q: Two shooters tie for 5th place. How are they ranked?

options.text: By a 25-target shoot-off for that place
By drawing lots after the event has ended
They share it; countback from the 8th layout or Compak sets the order
By age, with the younger shooter placed higher

questions.explain: Shoot-offs are only for the top three. Below that, tied shooters share the place, and countback compares the 8th layout or Compak, then the 7th, and so on.

questions.q: In Compak in line, when do you count as late?

options.text: When your number is cancelled in the system and the next shooter is on station 1
As soon as the referee has called out your name for the first time
Only after the whole group has finished shooting the round

questions.explain: Both things must have happened: your number is already cancelled in the computer system, and the next shooter stands on station 1. The penalty is 25 zeros for the round.

questions.q: How do you carry your gun between stands?

options.text: Open, so everyone can see it is not loaded, and without a sling
Closed and unloaded, on a sling over your shoulder
Closed, with the safety catch on, pointing at the ground

questions.explain: Guns are carried open and slings are not allowed; a semi-automatic is carried with its breech open.

questions.q: Which gun is NOT allowed in FITASC Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting?
questions.explain: Pump-action guns are banned; the others are allowed if they meet the gauge and barrel limits.

questions.q: How many cartridges may a semi-automatic hold?

options.text: As many as the magazine takes

questions.explain: Both rulebooks limit a semi-automatic to two cartridges.

questions.q: Why do most competition shooters choose an over-and-under?

options.text: It has the softest recoil of any type of gun
The rules allow no other type of competition gun
It is the cheapest gun that you can buy
An open O/U is easy to check and takes two chokes

questions.explain: Visible safety, two chokes and reliability are the main reasons. Many shooters find a gas semi-automatic softer.

questions.q: What must a semi-automatic have in Compak® Sporting?

options.text: A device that stops cases hitting the neighbour
A sling so it can be carried safely
A magazine for at least five cartridges
A red sticker with the letter 'S'

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting a shell catcher or deflector is compulsory, and slings are banned.

questions.q: What is the shortest barrel length the FITASC rules allow?
questions.explain: Barrels must be at least 66 cm long in both disciplines.

questions.q: A client asks why pumps are banned. What is the honest answer?

options.text: The rules state the ban without explaining it
The rulebook says they are too slow for doubles
The rulebook says they are less safe
They are in fact allowed in Compak® Sporting

questions.explain: The rulebooks give no reason; as an interpreter, report the rule and do not invent explanations.

questions.q: Which choke gives the widest pattern?
questions.explain: Cylinder has no constriction, so the shot spreads soonest.

questions.q: What happens if you increase the constriction?

options.text: The pattern stays tighter for longer
The shot leaves the barrel faster

questions.explain: More constriction keeps the shot together longer, so at the same distance the pattern is narrower and denser.

questions.q: Why is a very open choke a poor choice for a far target?

options.text: It gives far more recoil than others
It is banned for targets over 30 m
At range the pattern thins out, with gaps
It wears the barrel out much faster

questions.explain: A wide pattern thins out at long range, and the target can slip between the pellets.

questions.q: What is a choke?

options.text: A narrowing of the barrel at the muzzle
The safety catch behind the top lever
A type of cartridge for clay targets
The top edge of the stock, for the cheek

questions.explain: A choke narrows the bore at the muzzle and keeps the shot together.

questions.q: In Sporting™, a shooter already standing on the stand wants to change a choke. Is it allowed?

options.text: Yes, as long as it causes no delay
No, not once he is on the stand
Yes, but only before the doubles

questions.explain: Changes are allowed between stands or between singles and doubles, without delay, but not once the shooter has stepped onto the stand.

questions.q: What ignites the powder in a cartridge?
questions.explain: The firing pin strikes the primer, which ignites the powder.

questions.q: Why do many grounds require fibre wads?
questions.explain: Fibre and felt break down, while ordinary plastic wads stay in the fields for years.

questions.q: Which cartridges do the FITASC rules ban?

options.text: Factory loads with a plastic wad
Factory loads with a fibre wad

questions.explain: Reloaded cartridges, dispersers, mixed shot, black powder and tracers are banned.

questions.q: What is the crimp of a cartridge?

options.text: The folded top that closes the hull
The metal head with the primer
The cup that holds the pellets
The number printed on the box

questions.explain: The crimp, most often a star of 6 or 8 folds, closes the top of the hull above the shot.

questions.q: What size is a mini target usually?
questions.explain: A mini is usually 60 mm and a midi 90 mm. Names of small targets vary, so go by the millimetres on the menu.

questions.q: On a Sporting™ stand, a trap throws a midi instead of the standard shown on the menu. What happens?

options.text: No Bird, the target is repeated

questions.explain: In Sporting™ a target of the wrong colour, size or type is a No Bird (it does not count) and is thrown again.

questions.q: Which target rolls along the ground?
questions.explain: The rabbit has a thick rim and is thrown on its edge along the ground.

questions.q: The menu says '70 mm'. The coach calls it a mini. What should you translate?

options.text: Correct it to 60 mm, since a mini is 60 mm
Keep the coach's word and the 70 mm on the menu
Call it a midi, since it is over 60 mm
Ask the coach to say 'super mini' instead

questions.explain: The rules name 70 mm and 60 mm sizes and the name 'super mini'; trust the millimetres on the menu and do not correct the coach.

questions.q: Which target flies edge-on, then turns to show its face and drops?
questions.explain: The battue is flat and thin: it flies edge-on, then turns and drops quickly.

questions.q: Which target leaves a cloud of coloured powder when it is hit?
questions.explain: A flash target is filled with coloured powder. It is scored like any other target.

questions.q: What do the rules require of a target's colour?

options.text: It must always be orange or white
It must stand out against the background
It must be two colours for contrast
Any colour: the rules say nothing

questions.explain: Visibility against the background is the requirement; two-colour targets are not recommended.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting it starts to rain hard and a shooter misses. Can he ask for a No Bird because of the weather?

options.text: Only for the first target of a double
Only if the jury agrees to it
No, weather is not a reason for a No Bird

questions.explain: The Compak® Sporting rules say bad weather is not a reason for a No Bird: the miss stays a miss. Separately, the Head Referee may stop the shoot for a sudden storm that looks short.

questions.q: A coach says 'Watch the orange one.' What is he describing?
questions.explain: Colour is chosen for visibility and says nothing about size or type.

questions.q: Which presentation usually needs the most lead?

options.text: An incomer flying straight at the shooter
A crosser at the same distance

questions.explain: All of a crosser's speed is sideways, so you shoot furthest in front of it; targets flying straight away from you or towards you need little sideways lead.

questions.q: A target comes towards the shooter at an angle and passes to the side. What is it called?
questions.explain: Quartering towards (or quartering in) is an angled target coming in; quartering away is the angled target moving off.

questions.q: Why should a target be read from the exact stand you will shoot from?

options.text: One trap can give a different angle from each stand
The rules forbid watching from any other place
Targets change colour from one stand to the next
Only the referee may stand anywhere else

questions.explain: The angle between the shooter and the target's line changes with the position, so the presentation changes too.

questions.q: A crosser flies far from you. Compared with a near one at the same speed, it needs…
questions.explain: The further the target, the further it travels while the shot is on its way, so it needs more lead.

questions.q: A crosser is slowing down at your break point. Compared with one at full speed, it needs…
questions.explain: A slower target moves less while the shot travels, so it needs less lead.

questions.q: From whose point of view are “left” and “right” given for a crosser?
questions.explain: Directions are the shooter's: an L→R crosser flies from the shooter's left to right.

questions.q: The coach says “long crosser”. What does “long” mean?

options.text: The target flies for a long time
The target is a long, oval clay
The shooter should wait a long time

questions.explain: In coaching “long” describes distance. A long crosser is a far crosser, which needs more lead.

questions.q: What is true of crossers in Compak® Sporting?

options.text: Crossers are not allowed on a Compak
Crossers may only be thrown as rabbits
An L→R and an R→L crosser are compulsory

questions.explain: The Compak® Sporting rules make three trajectories compulsory: an L→R crosser, an R→L crosser and a going-away target.

questions.q: How does the lead on a quartering target compare with a full crosser at the same distance and speed?

options.text: It is the same as the crosser
It is larger than the crosser
It is smaller, depending on the angle

questions.explain: Only the sideways part of the movement needs sideways lead, so the closer the target is to a straight line away from you or towards you, the smaller the lead.

questions.q: The coach says: “Blot it out.” What should the shooter do?

options.text: Wipe the lenses of the safety glasses
Let the barrels cover the target at the shot
Wait until the target disappears from view
Shoot only at the falling pieces

questions.explain: On incomers, driven and rising targets the gun often covers the clay at the moment of the shot; the coach asks for exactly that.

questions.q: Why should a going-away target not be left too long?

options.text: It quickly gets further away and smaller
The rules allow only three seconds
It always turns into a crosser
The referee calls No Bird after the peak

questions.explain: A going-away target gains distance fast, so the longer you wait, the harder it becomes. Three seconds is the release time, not a shooting limit.

questions.q: What makes a driven target different from an ordinary incomer?

options.text: It comes from behind the shooter
It passes over the shooter's head
It is thrown only in Compak® Sporting

questions.explain: Driven means an incomer that comes over the head, like driven game. A target coming from behind is an overhead from behind.

questions.q: Which target is thrown almost straight up, stalls at the top and falls back?
questions.explain: That is the teal (springing or rising teal). A looper flies a wide arc across the sky.

questions.q: Where does the lead usually go on a dropping target?

options.text: Only to the side, not down

questions.explain: A falling target moves down as well as along, so part of the lead is vertical: below and ahead.

questions.q: A French-speaking coach says “chandelle”. What is the safest thing to do?

options.text: Check: straight up, or an arc over the top?
Ignore it, since it is not a rulebook term

questions.explain: French speakers often mean an almost vertical target (an English teal), while an English setter’s chandelle climbs on a curve and arcs over; a quick check avoids a wrong plan.

questions.q: Which target flies a wide arc across the sky, like a rainbow?
questions.explain: A looper climbs, rolls over the top and falls on a wide arc. A teal goes almost straight up.

questions.q: The first shot misses a rabbit, then it breaks on a stone before the second shot. What happens?

options.text: It is scored as a hit, since it broke
It is scored zero for the first miss
No Bird: repeated, only a second-shot break counts
The shooter just moves to the next target

questions.explain: Both rulebooks treat this as a No Bird; on the repeat the shooter must deliberately miss with the first shot.

questions.q: Why do coaches warn against too much lead on a rabbit?

options.text: It is heavy and slows quickly
It is smaller than a mini

questions.explain: A rabbit has a thick rim and rolls on the ground, losing speed fast. So the lead you would give a flying crosser sends the shot ahead of the rabbit: a miss in front.

questions.q: What does “fur and feather” mean?

options.text: A pair of a rabbit and an aerial target
A target with feathers glued on

questions.explain: In British coaches’ slang “fur” is the rabbit and “feather” the flying target.

questions.q: May you shoot a rabbit from the hip in Sporting™?

options.text: No, each target is shot from the shoulder
Yes, if the referee does not object

questions.explain: The rules require each target, rabbits included, to be shot with the gun mounted.

questions.q: In a report pair, what releases the second target?

options.text: The shot at the first target

questions.explain: “On report” means on the sound of the shot: firing at the first target releases the second.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting a shooter deliberately fires both cartridges at the first target of a simultaneous double. Result?

options.text: Only the second target is zero

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting allows one cartridge per target of a double; deliberately firing both at one target is scored zero-zero. In Sporting™ it would be allowed.

questions.q: In which discipline are there rafale doubles?
questions.explain: A rafale is two targets from one trap on one trajectory, a Sporting™ double. Compak® Sporting has only doubles on report and simultaneous doubles.

questions.q: A British coach says “true pair”. How do you translate it?
questions.explain: “True pair” is what British coaches call a simultaneous pair; “true” has nothing to do with correctness.

questions.q: How many targets does one Sporting™ layout give?
questions.explain: Each Sporting™ layout type gives 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles.

questions.q: In Sporting™ one shot breaks both targets of a double. How is it scored?

options.text: No Bird, the double is repeated

questions.explain: In Sporting™ both targets count when one shot breaks them. Compak® Sporting has different rules.

questions.q: Where does the coach usually want the front foot to point?
questions.explain: Feet set to the break point keep the body relaxed where the shot happens. If the feet face the trap, the body cannot turn far enough to reach the break point.

questions.q: What do the Sporting™ rules require of the feet before the call?

options.text: The front foot on the stand line

questions.explain: The ready-position rule asks for both feet inside the 1 m shooting stand before the shooter calls.

questions.q: A left-handed shooter. The coach says “Open your front foot”. Which foot is it?

options.text: The left one, whatever the hand
The right one: a left-hander's front foot
The back foot, nearer the trap

questions.explain: For a left-hander the front foot is the right one. Translating “front foot” as front, not as left, avoids the mistake.

questions.q: How does a right-handed shooter usually place the feet?
questions.explain: A right-hander puts the left foot slightly forward, a left-hander the right.

questions.q: Which point should your feet be set up for?
questions.explain: Then your body turns easily to exactly where you will break the target.

questions.q: Where must the shooter’s feet be in Sporting™ before calling?
questions.explain: The Sporting™ rules require both feet inside the shooting stand before the call.

questions.q: In Sporting™, until when must the stock stay below the vest line?

options.text: Until the referee gives a nod
Until the target is out and visible
Until the first shot is fired

questions.explain: The ready position is held until the target has been released and can be seen; only then may the gun be mounted.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, may a shooter call for the target with the gun already at the shoulder?

options.text: No: it earns a yellow card
Only for rabbits and other low targets
Only between the two targets of a double
Yes: the gun position at the call is free

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting has no low-gun rule: the gun may be mounted or not at the call, but each target is shot from the shoulder.

questions.q: Why do coaches insist on the cheek staying on the comb?

options.text: The eye works as the rear sight, so it must sit in one place
To reduce the noise reaching the ear
Because the rules of both disciplines require it
To hide the face from the referee

questions.explain: A shotgun has no rear sight: your eye does that job, so a lifted cheek sends the shot high.

questions.q: Which is right during the mount?

options.text: The face goes to the gun
The gun comes to the face
The head bends to the rib

questions.explain: The head stays level and the gun comes to the cheek and shoulder.

questions.q: How far below the shoulder axis is the vest line drawn in Sporting™?
questions.explain: The line is drawn 25 cm below the shoulder axis, parallel to it.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, may you call for the target with the gun already mounted?

options.text: Yes, the position at the call is free
No, only from a low gun position

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free; the low gun with a vest line is a Sporting™ rule.

questions.q: A right-handed shooter has a left dominant eye. What is this called?
questions.explain: Cross-dominance is a dominant eye on the opposite side to the shooting shoulder.

questions.q: Why is looking back at the bead to check the lead a fault?

options.text: It is forbidden by the rules of both disciplines
It usually slows or stops the gun, so the shot goes behind
The bead reflects the sun into the eye
It makes the target change colour in flight

questions.explain: When you look at the gun instead of the target, the swing tends to slow or stop. The target slips to the edge of your vision, and the shot goes behind.

questions.q: Where does the anti-dominance dot usually go?

options.text: On the safety glasses, in front of one eye
On the bead at the end of the rib
On the rib, halfway along it
On the vest line, below the shoulder

questions.explain: Safety glasses are compulsory anyway, so a small dot on the lens in front of the non-dominant eye is the simplest remedy.

questions.q: What does the hand-triangle test show?
questions.explain: The eye that keeps the object in the triangle is the master eye.

questions.q: A right-handed shooter has a left master eye. What is it called?
questions.explain: A master eye on the other side from the stock is cross-dominance.

questions.q: Who should help you decide how to shoot with cross-dominance?

options.text: Another squad member during a competition

questions.explain: A coach will take into account your age, experience and how strong the dominance is. Besides, coaching during a competition is not allowed.

questions.q: Which point is about the eyes, not the gun?
questions.explain: The pick-up point is where the eyes first see the target clearly; the hold point is for the muzzles.

questions.q: What usually happens if the hold point is too close to the trap?

options.text: The gun has to chase the target
The gun has almost no room to move

questions.explain: Too near the trap, the target leaves at full speed past the muzzles, so the gun has to chase it. Too little room to move is the problem of a hold point too far out.

questions.q: In Sporting™, the shooter on the stand asks to see the presentation again. What is the maximum per target of the menu?

options.text: As many as the shooter wants

questions.explain: The referee will show it again if asked, but no more than twice per target on the menu.

questions.q: What is the hold point?

options.text: Where the barrels wait when you call

questions.explain: The hold point is where you hold the muzzles before calling.

questions.q: Where do your eyes go before calling?
questions.explain: Your eyes wait where the target first becomes clearly visible.

questions.q: Which point are your feet set for?
questions.explain: Feet are set for the break point, so the body is most comfortable there.

questions.q: The coach says “You stopped the gun”. Where did the shot most likely go?
questions.explain: The target keeps moving while the stopped gun does not, so the shot passes behind it.

questions.q: Which gun speed describes maintained lead?
questions.explain: In maintained lead the muzzles move at the target's speed, keeping the gap constant. A waiting gun is ambush; faster is swing-through.

questions.q: What is the difference between tempo and rhythm?

options.text: Tempo is the speed of the shot, rhythm its evenness
They are two words for the same thing
Tempo is the music played on the ground
Rhythm is the time limit between targets

questions.explain: Coaches change the tempo for each target while keeping a smooth rhythm, so translate both words separately.

questions.q: What is follow-through?

options.text: The gun keeps moving after the shot
A second shot at the same target
Checking the gun before a round

questions.explain: The movement does not end at the shot but continues along the target's line for a moment.

questions.q: Where does the shot usually go if the shooter stops the gun?
questions.explain: Stopped barrels fall behind the target, and the shot passes behind it.

questions.q: What often causes a shot over the target?

options.text: Lifting the head off the stock
A cartridge that is too heavy

questions.explain: When the head comes up, the eye no longer looks along the rib, and the gun shoots high.

questions.q: What is perceived lead?

options.text: The real distance in front of the clay in the air
The gap the shooter sees between muzzle and target
The lead written on the target menu
The distance from the stand to the trap

questions.explain: Perceived lead is the picture at the muzzle; actual lead is the real distance in the air and is much larger.

questions.q: Of the methods with a moving gun, which usually gives the largest perceived lead?
questions.explain: With maintained lead the gun moves no faster than the target, so nothing is added on its own and you have to see the whole gap. With ambush, where the gun is still, the gap seen is even bigger.

questions.q: Which target needs almost no sideways lead?
questions.explain: A straight going-away target has no sideways movement; any lead it needs is vertical.

questions.q: Why do you need lead?

options.text: So that shot and target meet
To make the target fly slower

questions.explain: While the shot flies the target moves on, so you shoot in front of it.

questions.q: In which method do the barrels stay in front of the target throughout?
questions.explain: Maintained lead: the barrels start in front and keep the gap.

questions.q: Which target needs the least lead?
questions.explain: A target going straight away or coming straight in hardly moves sideways relative to the barrels.

questions.q: With which method must the shooter see the biggest gap at the moment of decision?
questions.explain: With ambush the gun is still, and the target keeps moving during the reaction time. So the gap seen at the decision must be bigger than the actual lead.

questions.q: In maintained lead, where do the muzzles join the target's line?
questions.explain: The muzzles are inserted ahead of the target and stay ahead; behind is swing-through, on the target is pull-away.

questions.q: What is the typical fault of maintained-lead shooters?

options.text: Measuring the gap and stopping the gun
Shooting too early at the trap

questions.explain: The gap is large and visible, so shooters are tempted to check it; the gun slows or stops and the shot goes behind.

questions.q: For which target is maintained lead often recommended?

options.text: A bouncing rabbit in a short gap

questions.explain: The method needs a known speed and line, which long, steady crossers give; erratic or surprise targets suit other methods.

questions.q: Where do the muzzles start in swing-through?

options.text: At a fixed point at the break point
Behind the target, on its line

questions.explain: Swing-through starts behind and overtakes the target; starting in front is maintained lead, a fixed point is ambush.

questions.q: Why does a swing-through shooter see little or no lead?

options.text: The gun's speed creates the lead
The rules forbid a visible gap

questions.explain: The gun moves faster than the target, so between deciding and firing it travels ahead by itself.

questions.q: A coach says “bum, belly, beak, bang”. What does “bum” mean here?
questions.explain: It means the tail of the target. A neutral word for “tail” keeps both the meaning and the rhythm of the memory aid.

questions.q: In pull-away, what happens just before the trigger is pulled?

options.text: The gun stops on the target
The gun accelerates ahead of the target
The gun drops below the target
The gun waits at the break point

questions.explain: The pull-away itself is the acceleration ahead; the shot is fired while the gun is still moving forward.

questions.q: The coach says “You rode it too long”. What went wrong?

options.text: He stood too long on the stand before calling
He mounted the gun far too early
He tracked it too long before pulling away
The trapper released the target late

questions.explain: “Riding the target” means following it too long, so it slows, drops or escapes and the line is lost.

questions.q: Compared with maintained lead, the perceived lead in pull-away is usually…

options.text: smaller, because the acceleration adds lead
larger, because the gun starts on the target
zero, with no gap at all

questions.explain: The brief acceleration carries the gun forward during the shot delay, so less gap needs to be seen.

questions.q: What characterises ambush (spot shooting)?

options.text: The gun swings faster than the target
The gun waits at a point ahead of the target
The gun tracks the target, then accelerates
The gun starts behind the target, on its line

questions.explain: Ambush means little or no swing: the muzzles wait on the line and the target flies into the shot.

questions.q: When can a deliberate ambush be a good choice?

options.text: In no case: the rules forbid it
Only in Compak® Sporting, not in Sporting™
On a rabbit seen only in a short gap

questions.explain: When the target is visible only briefly, there is no time for a swing, so waiting at the gap can work. No rule forbids any method.

questions.q: What is instinctive shooting?

options.text: Hard focus on the target, no conscious lead
Shooting from the hip, without mounting
Waiting at the trap for each target

questions.explain: Instinctive shooting relies on eye–hand coordination; it is still done with the gun at the shoulder, as the rules require.

questions.q: The coach says “Give it four foot” to a shooter who thinks in metres. What do you say?
questions.explain: A lead number is the coach’s picture. Converting it mid-instruction adds false precision or errors, and “four metres” changes the meaning completely. If the shooter asks, explain roughly between targets.

questions.q: What does “half a bird” mean?

options.text: Half the width of a target
A target that broke in two
A small bird near the trap

questions.explain: In clay shooting “bird” means the target, so the coach asks for half a target’s width of lead.

questions.q: The coach says “Same lead, keep it moving”. Why must “same lead” be translated?

options.text: It is a call the referee uses
Otherwise the shooter may add lead and miss
It is a polite greeting between shooters
It changes the order of the targets

questions.explain: After a miss many shooters add lead by themselves. “Same lead” tells them the cause was the stopped gun, not the lead.

questions.q: A target flies from right to left. The coach says “You were at two o’clock.” Where did the shot cloud (the pattern) go?

options.text: Low and in front of the target
High and in front of the target

questions.explain: Two o’clock on the target is up and to the right. On a target going right to left, its right side is behind it, so the pattern was high and behind.

questions.q: The coach calls: 'Behind, you stopped!' What matters most for the next shot?

options.text: Nothing: you saw the miss yourself
A request to add a lot more lead

questions.explain: Adding lead does not cure a stopped gun; the cause is what the shooter has to fix.

questions.q: A small but clearly visible piece breaks off the clay. The coach says 'just chipped it'. How does the referee score it?

options.text: Lost, because most of the clay flew on
Hit only if the coach agrees

questions.explain: At least one visible piece makes the target a hit in both Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting; the referee decides alone.

questions.q: After a hit the coach shouts 'Smoked it!'. What does he mean?

options.text: Only dust came off, so it is lost

questions.explain: In coach slang 'smoked it' is praise for a clay turned to dust, and the rules count that as a hit too. Only an intact clay that gives off a puff of dust or smoke, with no visible piece, is a zero.

questions.q: The coach says 'You lifted your head'. Where did the shot most likely go?
questions.explain: Your eye does the job of a rear sight (a shotgun has none): when the head lifts, the shot usually goes over.

questions.q: A coach shouts 'Stop aiming!'. What does he want?

options.text: Don't point like a rifle: look at the target and swing
Aim more carefully along the rib at the clay
Stop shooting and open the gun at once
Lower the gun and wait for the referee

questions.explain: 'Aiming' in a coach's mouth is a fault (poking); the cure is eyes on the clay and a free swing.

questions.q: 'You rode it too long' means…

options.text: The trap threw the target too slowly
The shooter started too far behind
The shooter followed the clay too long

questions.explain: Riding the target means following it too long, so it slows or drops and the line is lost.

questions.q: In training, a coach tells a shooter preparing for a FITASC Sporting™ competition: 'Pre-mount this one.' What is true?

options.text: Allowed in competition too, if the referee is told first
A rule change: the low gun is no longer needed in Sporting™
A training drill; in competition, mount after the target appears
A Compak® Sporting rule that applies to all FITASC disciplines

questions.explain: Sporting™ requires the gun-down ready position until the target appears; a pre-mount in competition earns a warning with a yellow card.

questions.q: 'You canted the gun' means…

options.text: The gun was tilted sideways at the shot
The gun reached the shoulder too late
The gun stopped moving at the shot
The safety catch was still on at the call

questions.explain: Canting is a sideways tilt of the gun, which pulls the shot off the line.

questions.q: Which instruction cures 'face to the gun'?

options.text: Bring the gun to your face
Hold the gun lower on the arm

questions.explain: The stock should come up to the face, so the eye is in the same place each time.

questions.q: What does 'eyes first, then the gun' mean on a pair?

options.text: Close the eyes after the first shot
Look at the barrel before the second shot
Mount the gun before calling for the pair
Find the second target with the eyes first

questions.explain: In a good transition the eyes lead and the gun follows.

questions.q: In a Compak® Sporting double, the shooter misses the first target and wants to fire the second cartridge at it too. Is that allowed?

options.text: Yes, the same as in Sporting™
Yes, but only on a simultaneous double
No: only one cartridge per target

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting forbids doubling the first target in a double; Sporting™ allows both cartridges at one target.

questions.q: In a Sporting™ double, may the shooter lower the gun between the first and the second target?

options.text: Yes, it is free between the two targets
No, the gun must stay at the shoulder
Only on a double on report
Only if the referee allows it

questions.explain: The free position applies between the targets of any double, but not before the first one.

questions.q: The coach asks the shooter “Where did it go?”. What should the interpreter do?

options.text: Translate the question, then the shooter’s answer exactly
Explain the miss in your own words
Say nothing: it is a rhetorical question

questions.explain: The coach wants to hear what the shooter actually saw, so the answer must reach him unchanged.

questions.q: During a competition the shooter’s coach asks you to pass on: “Give the next one more lead.” What is the safe practice?

options.text: Pass it on quietly, in a whisper
Pass it on, but only between stands
Decline: coaching is not allowed in competition

questions.explain: Coaching in competition is forbidden, and the rules do not say whether an interpreter may relay it; staying out of it protects the shooter.

questions.q: What do the rules say happens if the referee judges that a competitor is being coached?

options.text: Yellow card; the coach is sent away

questions.explain: Both rulebooks give the competitor a yellow card, with heavier penalties for repeats, and the referee removes the coach from the shooting area.

questions.q: The coach says “It’s about thirty yards.” How can you pass it on to a shooter who thinks in metres?
questions.explain: A yard is a little less than a metre (about 0.9 m), so thirty yards is about 27 m. Keep “about”: the coach’s number is an estimate.

questions.q: What is the largest calibre allowed in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting?
questions.explain: Both rulebooks allow calibre 12 at most; a smaller gauge number means a wider bore, so 10 is not allowed.

questions.q: A British guest asks whether his “one-ounce” cartridges are legal at a FITASC event. What do you know?

options.text: Any load: there is no limit
A 28 g load (+2%), about one ounce

questions.explain: The rules allow a load of up to 28 g with a +2% tolerance, and one ounce is about 28.3 g. The shot size (2.0–2.5 mm) must also fit.

questions.q: The coach says “Don’t ride it.” What does he mean?

options.text: Put more weight on your front foot
Do not follow the target too long
Do not mount the gun too early

questions.explain: “Riding” a target means tracking it too long to be sure. The target slows, drops or curls away, and the gun often stops.

questions.q: How should an interpreter translate “Stare it to death”?

options.text: Word for word, keeping the image
Leave it out: it is only a joke
By its meaning: look hard at the target
As a warning about the referee

questions.explain: Pass on the meaning, not the picture: the coach wants intense, unbroken focus on the target.

questions.q: After a miss the coach says “Let it go, next target.” What is the message?

options.text: Accept the miss; focus on the next one
Change the order of the targets
Let the next shooter go first

questions.explain: Accept the miss, do a short reset and give the next target your full routine; many coaches leave the analysis for after the round.

questions.q: How far below the shoulder axis (an imaginary line through both shoulders) is the vest line in Sporting™?
questions.explain: The line runs 25 cm below the shoulder axis, parallel to it.

questions.q: May you call for the target in Compak® Sporting with the gun already at the shoulder?

options.text: No, the gun must start low

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting has no low-gun rule and no vest line; only the shot itself must be fired from the shoulder.

questions.q: When may you hold the gun as you like in Sporting™?

options.text: Between the two targets of a double
Before the first target of a double

questions.explain: The free position is allowed only between the two targets of a double; before the first one the ready position applies.

questions.q: On the first stand, a shooter calls with the gun already at the shoulder. It is the first such offence on this layout. What does the referee decide?

options.text: A warning and a yellow card

questions.explain: The first gun-position offence is a verbal warning backed by a yellow card.

questions.q: Earlier on this layout, a shooter got a yellow card for gun position. Now, on a single, the stock is above the vest line at the call. Decision?
questions.explain: After the warning, a further offence on the same layout is a red card: zero on a single.

questions.q: Sporting™. The referee has already warned a shooter once for mock shooting. Before the next call, the shooter again mounts and swings along the target's line, then breaks the target. How is it scored?
questions.explain: After a first warning for mock shooting, a repeat costs the next target the shooter hits: it is scored zero.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting a shooter calls with the gun held low and, when the rabbit appears, fires from the hip without mounting. Is that allowed?

options.text: Yes, the gun position is free
No, each shot is fired from the shoulder
Yes, but only at a rabbit

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting you may call with the gun up or down, but each target must be shot with the gun at the shoulder.

questions.q: A Sporting™ shooter uses a Monte Carlo stock, with a raised comb. Does the vest-line rule apply?

options.text: Yes, it covers each type of stock

questions.explain: The rule covers standard, Monte Carlo and adjustable-comb stocks: before the target appears, the top back of the stock stays below the vest line, which runs 25 cm below the shoulder axis.

questions.q: Within how many seconds of the call must the target be released?
questions.explain: In both disciplines a target released more than 3 seconds late is a No Bird.

questions.q: How long do you have to call in Compak® Sporting?
questions.explain: You have at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target. In Sporting™ you have at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles.

questions.q: A target is released although you did not call for it. What is it?
questions.explain: A target you did not call for is a No Bird, and it is the only kind you may refuse.

questions.q: The shooter calls and the referee relays the signal, but the target leaves about five seconds later. Decision?
questions.explain: The target must leave within three seconds of the referee's signal; a later one is a No Bird and is thrown again.

questions.q: A shooter arrives while the squad is still shooting singles on stand 1, before their turn has come. What happens?

options.text: Zero on all singles of stand 1
They must shoot with another squad

questions.explain: If you arrive before your turn on the singles of the first stand has passed, there is no penalty.

questions.q: Between two singles a shooter takes about 25 seconds, for the first time today. Decision?
questions.explain: The limit is 15 seconds; the first time it is exceeded the referee warns, and only then do penalties follow.

questions.q: Compak® Sporting with a sonopull. The target leaves half a second after the shooter's call. Is that a No Bird?
questions.explain: A sonopull always releases the target half a second after the call. Only a target more than 3 seconds late is a No Bird.

questions.q: For the second time in the same round, a shooter takes more than 10 seconds to call. The target is a single. Decision?
questions.explain: After the first warning, a repeat in the same round is penalised by the table: a single is scored zero.

questions.q: Compak® Sporting by squad. A shooter arrives a moment after the squad's first shooter has called the round's first target. What follows?

options.text: Shoots at the end of the squad

questions.explain: The deadline is the squad's first call. After it, the late shooter gets 25 zeros; a written appeal to the jury on the same day is possible.

questions.q: In Sporting™, which doubles are NOT shown at the presentation?
questions.explain: In Sporting™ doubles on report are not presented; simultaneous and rafale doubles are. A double only uses targets already thrown as singles on that stand.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting by squad, how often are the targets presented?

options.text: Before each squad, on each station
Once a day, for the first squad
Only when a shooter asks for it

questions.explain: There is one presentation a day, in the morning, for the first squad; after a break of more than 10 minutes the referee presents the six singles once more.

questions.q: In Sporting™, during the presentation a shooter closes the gun and swings along a target's line. What applies?

options.text: Forbidden: a warning, then a red card
Only the coach gets a warning

questions.explain: Guns stay open during the presentation, and firing or mock shooting is penalised like a gun-position offence.

questions.q: In Sporting™, how many repeats may the shooter on the stand ask for?
questions.explain: On request the referee shows a target again, at most twice for each target on the menu.

questions.q: Compak® Sporting in line, with doubles on report. While the line is filling, a new shooter steps onto station 1. What does the referee show this shooter?

options.text: The first target of their double

questions.explain: In line, the singles A to F are shown to the first shooter before the start. After that, each new shooter on station 1 is shown the opening target of their double.

questions.q: May you practise on the competition trajectories before a Compak® Sporting event?

options.text: Only on the morning of the event

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting allows practice on the competition trajectories, but the setting tables (menus) for practice must differ; in Sporting™ practising on the competition layouts is not allowed for anyone.

questions.q: After the shot the target only gives off dust, and no piece is seen. What is the result?
questions.explain: A hit needs at least one visible piece; dust or smoke alone is a zero.

questions.q: Who decides whether a target was hit?
questions.explain: The referee decides alone and may ask others for advice only on his or her own initiative.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting heavy rain starts, and you miss. What is the result?

options.text: A No Bird, if you ask

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting a broken target is 'one' and a miss is 'zero' in any weather. Only the Head Referee may stop shooting for a sudden storm.

questions.q: A target of the wrong colour comes out of the trap. What is it?
questions.explain: A target of the wrong colour is a No Bird in both disciplines and is thrown again.

questions.q: A tiny chip flies off the target, and the rest of it flies on. What is the score?
questions.explain: Any visible piece that comes off makes it a hit, however small it is.

questions.q: After a 'lost' call, a squad member walks out to pick up the target and show the referee a chip on it. What do the rules say?

options.text: The referee must look at it
Not allowed: targets are not picked up

questions.explain: Nobody may pick up a target to check it, and squad members may not intervene: the referee decides alone.

questions.q: Your cartridge misfires. What do you do first?

options.text: Open the gun and check the cartridge
Reload at once and call again
Stay put, gun closed, and wait for the referee

questions.explain: Opening the gun or touching the safety before the referee's check means the target is scored zero.

questions.q: In Sporting™, a second gun malfunction happens in the same round, on a single. What is the result?
questions.explain: Only the first malfunction in a round is a No Bird; from the second, the target is scored zero.

questions.q: How long do you have in Compak® Sporting to repair or replace the gun?
questions.explain: You have two minutes; without a working gun, the targets not shot are zero.

questions.q: In training, with no referee, your gun clicks but does not fire. What should you do?

options.text: Open it at once and look
Keep it pointing safely and wait before opening
Turn around and show it to the coach

questions.explain: A cartridge can fire late (a hang fire), so keep the muzzle in a safe direction and wait before you open the gun. Your instructor or the ground's rules will say how long.

questions.q: After a misfire, you push the safety catch on before the referee has looked at the gun. What happens?
questions.explain: Touching the safety before the referee's check costs the target, just like opening the gun. Wait, gun pointing down the range.

questions.q: Why is a failed gun not opened at once?

options.text: So as not to dirty the cartridge
Because the cartridge may fire late

questions.explain: A hang fire is rare but dangerous, so the gun must stay pointed in a safe direction.

questions.q: Sporting™: your gun fails on a stand (first incident), and it is repaired while your squad is still shooting that stand. What may you do?

options.text: Shoot the stand last, if the referee allows
Nothing: the remaining targets are zero

questions.explain: If the gun is repaired before the squad has finished the stand, you may shoot it last there, with the referee's permission.

questions.q: First gun problem of the round: on a single the first cartridge misfires. The shooter waits, gun down range, for the referee. Decision?
questions.explain: In a round, the first incident with the gun or ammunition is a No Bird with a warning, and the single is repeated.

questions.q: The cartridge misfires, and the annoyed shooter breaks the gun open to look at the primer before the referee arrives. Decision?

options.text: The target is repeated after a warning
Red card, and the target is repeated

questions.explain: Opening the gun or touching the safety before the referee's check means the target is scored zero.

questions.q: Single, first incident: the first shot misses and the second cartridge misfires, so the target is repeated. On the repeat the shooter breaks it with the first shot. Decision?
questions.explain: After a second-shot failure the repeated single may only be broken with the second shot, so the first shot must be a deliberate miss.

questions.q: First incident of the round in Compak® Sporting: the first cartridge fails on a single. The shooter waits correctly. Decision?

options.text: No Bird and a yellow card

questions.explain: The first gun or cartridge incident in a round is a No Bird with a first warning shown by a yellow card.

questions.q: A shooter's gun breaks down, and they want to borrow a squad-mate's gun. Is it allowed?

options.text: No, only from outside the squad

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting forbids sharing a gun within a group. Exceptional borrowing is only from outside it, with the owner's and the referee's agreement.

questions.q: Second gun failure of the same type in this round, on a single the shooter could not shoot at. Decision?
questions.explain: From the second incident of the same type, targets not shot at are scored zero.

questions.q: What releases the second target of a double on report?

options.text: The shot at the first target
A second call by the shooter

questions.explain: The call releases the first target, and the shot at it releases the second.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, may you fire both cartridges at the first target of a double?
questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting it is one cartridge per target, and firing both at one target on purpose is scored zero-zero; in Sporting™ both may go at one target.

questions.q: In Sporting™, one shot breaks both targets of a double. How is it scored?
questions.explain: In Sporting™ both targets count; Compak® Sporting has different rules.

questions.q: Sporting™, simultaneous double. The shooter misses one target with the first shot, fires the second cartridge at the same target and breaks it. The other target flies on. Decision?

options.text: No Bird, the double is repeated

questions.explain: In Sporting™ both cartridges of a double may go at one target, so the broken target is 'one' and the other is 'zero'. In Compak® Sporting firing both at one target on purpose is scored zero-zero.

questions.q: Sporting™, double on report. The shooter breaks the first target, and a piece of it smashes the second before the second shot. Decision?
questions.explain: When the first target or its pieces break the second before the second shot, the double is repeated and the first result stands.

questions.q: Sporting™, rafale double. Both targets fly correctly, but the shooter lowers the gun and fires at neither, with no valid reason. Decision?
questions.explain: A correct target not fired at without a valid reason is lost; on a rafale or simultaneous double that means zero and zero.

questions.q: Simultaneous double in Compak® Sporting. One shot breaks both targets; it is the first time this has happened. Decision?
questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting a simultaneous double broken with one shot is a No Bird the first and second time, and zero and zero the third time.

questions.q: Double on report in Compak® Sporting. One shot breaks both targets. Decision?
questions.explain: In a double on report the first target's result is recorded, the second is a No Bird, and the double is shot again to score it.

questions.q: Compak® Sporting, double on report. The first target flies correctly, but the shooter does not fire at it. Decision?

options.text: First zero, double again for the second
Zero and zero for the double
No Bird, the double is thrown again
Zero, and the second is not shot

questions.explain: Not firing at a correctly thrown first target is a zero. The double is then thrown again so that the second target can be scored (referees' quick guide).

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, both barrels fire together by accident on the first target of a double. It is the first gun problem of the round. What is it?

options.text: A gun fault: No Bird, a new double

questions.explain: An accidental double discharge is a malfunction, not a deliberate double shot; zero-zero is only for firing both shots at one target on purpose.

questions.q: The referee sees a coach giving advice to a shooter during a competition. What do the rules say?

options.text: A red card for the coach
A yellow card for the shooter

questions.explain: Both rulebooks give the shooter a yellow card, and the person who coached has to leave the shooting area.

questions.q: Sporting™: after a yellow card for an early mount, the shooter mounts early again on the same layout, on a single. What follows?

options.text: A red card and a zero

questions.explain: After the first warning, doing it again on the same layout means a red card; on a single the target is zero.

questions.q: Which of these can the jury NOT impose under the penalty scale?

options.text: A cash fine to the referee

questions.explain: The jury can take away one target or a whole round, or exclude the shooter; there is no fine to the referee.

questions.q: How do you protest correctly on the stand?

options.text: Go to the jury after the round
Call the next target, then tell the referee
At once raise a hand and say 'protest' or 'appeal'

questions.explain: You protest at once, before the next call; calling the next target means accepting the ruling.

questions.q: What can be appealed to the jury?

options.text: Other rulings, not hit, miss or trajectory
Whether you really hit the target or not
Whether the trajectory was correct or not

questions.explain: Hit, miss, No Bird and trajectory are decided by the referee alone, and that decision is final.

questions.q: What is the deposit for a jury appeal in Sporting™?
questions.explain: It is 40% of the entry fee; the money comes back if the jury decides in the shooter's favour.

questions.q: Compak® Sporting: after the round, a shooter refuses to sign the score sheet because they disagree with one call. What is the consequence?

options.text: They lose the right to complain
The referee must change the result

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the shooter signs the score sheet at the end of each round; without the signature, no complaint can be accepted.

questions.q: Which shorts are allowed at FITASC competitions?
questions.explain: Short shorts are banned; long ones are allowed if they end no more than 5 cm above the knee.

questions.q: How many cartridges may a semi-automatic hold on the stand?
questions.explain: Both rulebooks limit a semi-automatic to no more than two cartridges.

questions.q: Are gun slings allowed in Compak® Sporting?
questions.explain: Slings and straps are banned in both disciplines; guns are carried open.

questions.q: A shooter arrives on the stand without safety glasses. What happens?
questions.explain: Glasses and ear protection are compulsory; without them the shooter may not shoot.

questions.q: Why are sandals banned?
questions.explain: Closed shoes protect the feet, so sandals are banned.

questions.q: Where is the competitor number worn?

options.text: On the front of the cap

questions.explain: The number is worn on your back, anywhere from the shoulders down to the waist, and nothing may hide any part of it.

questions.q: You are an interpreter standing near the stand. Must you wear ear protection?

options.text: No, only the shooters on the stand
Yes, everyone on or near a layout
Only if the referee asks you to

questions.explain: Hearing protection is compulsory for shooters, referees, staff and spectators.

questions.q: Which footwear is banned in both disciplines?
questions.explain: Sandals are forbidden for safety reasons.

questions.q: A shooter comes to the station in sandals for a practice round. Is it allowed?
questions.explain: The Compak® Sporting dress code bans sandals for safety, in practice and in competition.

questions.q: How do you protest correctly?

options.text: After the round, at the competition office
Call the next target, then explain why
At once on the stand: hand up, say “protest”

questions.explain: A protest is made immediately on the stand; in Sporting™ calling the next target means accepting the previous ruling.

questions.q: Which decision cannot be appealed to the jury?

options.text: Whether a target was one or zero

questions.explain: Hit or miss is decided by the stand referee alone, in both disciplines. Other referee decisions can go to the jury in writing.

questions.q: In Sporting™, how big is the deposit for a written appeal to the jury?
questions.explain: The Sporting™ rules set the deposit at 40% of the entry fee; it is returned if the jury agrees with the shooter.

questions.q: In Sporting™, your shooter thinks a target scored zero was hit, but has already called the next target. Can he still protest that ruling?

options.text: Yes, at the end of the round
Yes, in writing to the jury
No: calling the next target means accepting the previous ruling

questions.explain: By calling the next target the shooter accepts the previous ruling, and one/zero decisions cannot go to the jury at all.

questions.q: In Sporting™, which decision CAN be appealed to the jury?

options.text: Whether a target was one or zero
Another referee decision, such as a lateness penalty

questions.explain: In Sporting™ one/zero, No Bird and trajectory decisions are final; other referee decisions may go to the jury in writing with a deposit.

questions.q: In Sporting™, what happens to the deposit if the jury agrees with the shooter?

options.text: It is returned to the shooter
It is shared with the referee
