questions.explain: An upheld appeal gets the deposit back; a rejected one sends it to a charity chosen by the FITASC Chairman.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, how soon must you resume shooting after the referee’s final decision?
questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting you resume within 10 seconds, in Sporting™ within 15; otherwise it counts as a refusal to comply.

questions.q: How does a category differ from a class?

options.text: They mean the same thing in the rules
A category is by results, a class by age
A category is by age or sex, a class by results

questions.explain: Junior, Lady, Senior and Veteran are categories by age or sex; AA, A, B and C are national classes by average score.

questions.q: How are tied shooters below third place ranked?

options.text: They share it; countback from the 8th layout sets the order
By a shoot-off of 25 targets for the place
By drawing lots after the event has ended

questions.explain: There are no shoot-offs below third place: the place is shared and countback sets the order, from the 8th layout or Compak back to the 1st.

questions.q: A shooter born in 1971 enters a FITASC competition in 2027. Which category?
questions.explain: He turns 56 in 2027, so he is Senior from 1 January, whatever his birthday.

questions.q: How many targets are in the first round of a shoot-off?
questions.explain: A shoot-off is a round of 25 targets; if the scores are still level, sudden death follows.

questions.q: Two shooters tie for 7th place. What happens?

options.text: A coin toss by the jury
They share the place and are ordered by countback

questions.explain: Shoot-offs are only for places 1–3; below that, tied shooters are listed by countback from the eighth layout or Compak.

questions.q: From what age can women and girls enter the Lady category under FITASC rules?

options.text: From 1 January of the year they turn 13
From the day of their 18th birthday
From 1 January of the year they turn 21

questions.explain: Lady starts from the year of the 13th birthday, counted by year of birth.

questions.q: Does the Lady category have an upper age limit?

options.text: Yes, it ends at the age of 55
No, the FITASC table sets none
Yes, it ends at the age of 40

questions.explain: The FITASC table sets no upper limit for Lady.

questions.q: Do women shoot shorter or easier trajectories?

options.text: No, the targets are the same for all

questions.explain: The category affects only the ranking, not the targets.

questions.q: How should you translate the FITASC category “Senior” for a client?
questions.explain: In FITASC Senior is an age group of 56–65; the main adult category is Men.

questions.q: How many shooters are in a Men team in Sporting™?
questions.explain: Teams usually have three shooters, but the Men team in Sporting™ has four.

questions.q: On a FITASC score card, what does O mean?
questions.explain: On the standard FITASC card a hit is marked X and a miss O.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting your shooter refuses to sign the score sheet. What is the consequence?

options.text: He loses the right to make any complaint
The referee signs and nothing changes

questions.explain: The Compak® Sporting rules say a shooter who refuses to sign loses the right to complain.

questions.q: You want to compare the scores of two shooters. What is a fair way to do it?

options.text: Compare the percentages, whatever the length of the event
Compare only the highest round each of them shot
Compare them over the same number of targets, preferably at one event

questions.explain: The same percentage over a different number of targets, or at other grounds, is not the same test: layouts differ in difficulty.

questions.q: How are ties for the top three places settled?
questions.explain: For the top three there is a 25-target shoot-off, then sudden death.

questions.q: In Sporting™, when must you check your score on the card?

options.text: Only at the end of the day

questions.explain: Check your score when leaving each stand and raise any disagreement at once; later there is no appeal.

questions.q: In Sporting™, what does the referee do with the score card before the squad moves to the next stand?

options.text: Takes it to the jury straight away
Pins it on the central scoreboard

questions.explain: Before the squad moves on, the referee photographs the card and marks with an asterisk the shooter who carries it to the next stand.

questions.q: In Sporting™ you think the referee scored your hit as a zero. When must you protest?

options.text: At the end of the round, at the card
At once, before you call the next target
After the stand, in writing to the jury

questions.explain: Protest at once, on the stand, with a raised hand. Calling for the next target counts as accepting the last decision.

questions.q: Which of these counts as an attempt to influence the referee?

options.text: Asking calmly: “Was that a No Bird?”
Arguing on after shooting has resumed

questions.explain: A protest at once is your right, and calm questions are fine. Disputing a final decision after shooting resumes counts as an attempt to influence.

questions.q: After a miss in training the coach asks “What did you see?”. What helps him most?

options.text: Your honest picture, even if unsure

questions.explain: The coach looks for the cause of the miss, and your picture is the main clue. “I don’t know” is useful too.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, until when can you protest a referee’s call?

options.text: Until the end of the round
Until you sign the score sheet

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the protest comes at once, before the next shooter calls, with a raised arm and “Protest!” or “Appeal!”.

questions.q: What should stay the same in your routine from one target to the next?
questions.explain: The order of the steps matters more than the seconds; the delay after the call can vary anyway (in Sporting™, and in Compak® Sporting with a manual release).

questions.q: Where is the gun when you call in Sporting™?

options.text: Already mounted firmly at the shoulder
Anywhere: the gun position is free
Down, the stock below the vest line

questions.explain: In Sporting™ the gun stays down until the target is visible. In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free.

questions.q: A noise disturbs you before you call. What can you do?

options.text: Lower the gun, breathe out and start again
Call quickly, before the same noise comes back
Ask the referee to show the target again

questions.explain: Until you call, you can restart your routine, as long as you stay within the time limit.

questions.q: Why is a pre-shot routine useful in competition?

options.text: To fill the time before the call
To bring back your usual rhythm
To show the referee you are ready

questions.explain: A familiar routine helps you keep your usual tempo and technique under pressure.

questions.q: How much time do you have between singles or between doubles in Sporting™?
questions.explain: The limit in Sporting™ is 15 seconds; going over it first earns a warning.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, how long do you have to call after the previous station's target?
questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting you have at most 10 seconds; in Sporting™ the limit is 15 seconds between singles or between doubles.

questions.q: When may you load the gun?

options.text: On the way to the stand, to save time
On the stand, once the referee allows
Anywhere, as long as the safety is on

questions.explain: Load only on the stand, with the gun pointing down the range, once the referee has allowed shooting to start.

questions.q: What happens if someone coaches a shooter during a competition?

options.text: Nothing: advice from a coach is always allowed
The whole round is shot again at the end
A yellow card, and the coach is sent away

questions.explain: Coaching during a competition is not allowed in either discipline: the shooter gets a yellow card and the person coaching is sent out of the shooting area.

questions.q: A coach and a shooter share no language. What helps most in the first session?

options.text: Agreed anchor words and hand signals
A translation app during the routine

questions.explain: A small agreed vocabulary and the coach’s signals carry most of a session; long explanations and phones during the routine get in the way.

questions.q: At a competition, the shooter’s coach asks the interpreter to pass on a tip. What is the safe practice?

options.text: Pass it on quietly between targets
Pass it on with the referee’s nod
Pass it on only between stands
Decline: pass on only official words

questions.explain: Coaching during the competition is forbidden, and the rules do not mention interpreters. Passing on only the referee, the jury and the organiser protects the shooter.

questions.q: When should the coach and the interpreter talk to the shooter on the stand?
questions.explain: The shooter’s routine ends with the shot, and by the time the gun is closed it is well under way; words during it break the shooter’s focus.

questions.q: When is the safety briefing interpreted, and how?

options.text: Briefly, in a whisper, while they load
At the start, consecutively and in full
Only if one of the guests asks for it
After the first stand, in a summary

questions.explain: Safety comes first and must not be shortened; consecutive mode lets each rule land.

questions.q: The coach says “Behind it. Give it more.” Which rendering between targets is right?

options.text: A longer, gentler sentence with tips
Only the fix: “shoot a bit earlier”

questions.explain: Follow the coach: same length, same order, what went wrong plus what to change, nothing added.

questions.q: Why keep the same words for “pick-up point”, “hold point” and “break point” all day?

options.text: The rules require these exact words
So the coach can follow your language
So the guest learns three clear ideas
It does not matter which words you use

questions.explain: Using the same words each time helps the guest learn the three ideas; if you change the words, three ideas look like six.
